elements.quote: Methods A living systematic review.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly labels the study as a 'living systematic review', identifying it as a systematic review.
No explicit statement of the main objective or review question is present in the supplied abstract text.

elements.quote: Studies including at least 100 people with confirmed or clinically suspected COVID-19 at 12 weeks or more post onset were included.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main inclusion criterion (≥100 people and ≥12 weeks post onset).

elements.quote: Medline, CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research on COVID-19 database, LitCovid and Google Scholar were searched till 17 March 2021.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources searched and reports the date last searched (17 March 2021).

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using the tool produced by Hoy et al.
elements.reason: The abstract states the method used to assess risk of bias (the Hoy et al. tool).

elements.quote: Results were analysed using descriptive statistics and meta-analyses to estimate prevalence.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the methods used to present and synthesize results (descriptive statistics and meta-analyses).

The abstract text provided does not report the total number of included studies or participants nor summarize study characteristics; numbers appear elsewhere in the manuscript but are not present in the supplied abstract text.
The supplied abstract text does not present results for the main outcomes or provide numbers of studies/participants for outcomes.
Although meta-analyses were conducted in the review (described elsewhere), the abstract does not report any summary estimates or confidence/credible intervals.

elements.quote: Results were analysed using descriptive statistics and meta-analyses to estimate prevalence.
elements.reason: The abstract reports prevalence estimation and does not present comparisons between groups; therefore, indicating direction of effect between groups is not applicable in the abstract.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision) in the supplied text.
No general interpretation of the results or their important implications is provided in the supplied abstract text.
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding in the provided text.

elements.quote: The protocol was registered with PROSPERO and published in a peer- reviewed journal.
elements.reason: While the protocol registration with PROSPERO is mentioned elsewhere, the abstract does not provide the register name and registration number; no registration number is reported in the supplied abstract text.

elements.quote: Background While it is now apparent clinical sequelae (long COVID) may persist after acute COVID-19, their nature, frequency and aetiology are poorly characterised.
elements.reason: Explicitly describes the current state of knowledge and highlights important uncertainties about the nature, frequency and aetiology of long COVID.

elements.quote: We conducted a 'living' systematic review to provide frequently updated evidence on the symptoms and complications of long COVID.
elements.reason: States the purpose and importance of conducting this living systematic review to provide up-to-date evidence on long COVID symptoms and complications.

elements.quote: Systematic reviews conducted early during the COVID-­ 19 pandemic soon became redundant due to the rapidity with which new research was released.
elements.reason: Explains why earlier systematic reviews were insufficient and justifies the need for a living review updating evidence as new research emerges.
The review concerns characterization of long COVID (symptoms and complications), not evaluation of an intervention; no mechanism of action is relevant or discussed.
The review does not concern a complex intervention or delivery context, so a logic model is not applicable.

elements.quote: This study aims to regularly synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics, to help inform clinical management, rehabilitation strategies and interventional studies to improve long-­ term outcomes.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides an explicit statement of the review objective (to synthesise evidence on long COVID characteristics and inform clinical management etc.), but it does not present the objective using a formal question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, PECOS) as required by the item.

elements.quote: We conducted a 'living' systematic review to provide frequently updated evidence on the symptoms and complications of long COVID.
elements.reason: The review addresses characteristics, symptoms and complications of long COVID rather than effects of interventions; therefore specifying planned comparisons using PICO for intervention effects is not applicable.

elements.quote: Peer-­ reviewed studies were considered eligible if they included at least 100 people with laboratory confirmed and/or clinically diagnosed COVID-­ 19. Without a clear, internationally agreed case definition, we included studies that reported symptoms or outcomes assessed at 12 or more weeks post COVID-­ 19 onset. 6
elements.reason: The eligibility criteria specify key study characteristics: minimum sample size (>=100), case definition (laboratory confirmed and/or clinically diagnosed COVID-19) and minimum follow-up (>=12 weeks).

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: Medline and CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021.
elements.reason: The search time window (dissemination years covered) is specified. Additional supporting evidence: text_12 states 'There were no language restrictions.' and text_14 states data extraction was not performed for non-peer-reviewed preprints, indicating publication/report status criteria.
No retrieved text explicitly distinguishes excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations if no subset data were available. Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians.
elements.reason: The synthesis groups (hospitalised, non-hospitalised, mixed) are specified and linked to subgroup/meta-analyses addressing setting and other comparisons.

elements.quote: Studies were excluded if they included fewer than 100 participants, to avoid small study effects, 18 or the follow-­ up was unclear or less than 12 weeks post onset.
elements.reason: A clear rationale is provided for the sample-size restriction (to avoid small study effects) and for follow-up requirement, satisfying the requirement to justify notable restrictions; additional rationale for excluding non-peer-reviewed preprints is given in text_14.

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: Medline and CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021. Additionally, we searched Google Scholar on 17 March 2021, screening the first 500 titles.
elements.reason: The text explicitly reports the date (17 March 2021) when the databases and Google Scholar were last searched and gives a start date (1 January 2020) for the database coverage window.

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: Medline and CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021.
elements.reason: The bibliographic databases are named and platform/interface information is provided for some (CINAHL via EBSCO, Global Health via Ovid) and an overall coverage date range (1 Jan 2020 to 17 Mar 2021) is reported.

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: ... WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021.
elements.reason: Study registers/online COVID-19 repositories (WHO Global Research Database and LitCovid) are named and a date restriction/coverage window is reported.

elements.quote: Additionally, we searched Google Scholar on 17 March 2021, screening the first 500 titles.
elements.reason: The online source (Google Scholar) and the search date are reported but no URL for the site is provided.
No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies is reported in the provided text.
The types of individuals contacted to identify studies are not described in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: A 'backwards' snowball search was conducted of the references of systematic reviews.
elements.reason: The methods specify the type of reference lists examined (references of systematic reviews) for a backwards snowball search.

elements.quote: A 'backwards' snowball search was conducted of the references of systematic reviews.
elements.reason: The seed reports (references of systematic reviews) are specified, but no citation index/platform for forward/backward citation searching is named and a specific search date for this step is not reported (only the overall search date is given).
There is no information about consulting journals or conference proceedings, their dates covered, or search methods in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Full search terms are included in online supplemental file 1.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the complete search terms (i.e. the full search strategy) are provided in an online supplemental file, indicating the full strategy as actually run is reported (albeit in supplemental material).

elements.quote: The following databases were searched: Medline and CINAHL (EBSCO), Global Health (Ovid), WHO Global Research Database on COVID-­ 19 and LitCovid from 1 January 2020 to 17 March 2021. Additionally, we searched Google Scholar on 17 March 2021, screening the first 500 titles.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the databases searched, the date range (1 Jan 2020 to 17 Mar 2021) and a limit on Google Scholar (first 500 titles), which describes search limits; however, no justification linking these limits to the eligibility criteria is provided.
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of adaptations is reported in the provided evidence.
No information about use of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms is reported in the provided evidence.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided evidence.
There is no description of any validation of the search strategy, validation process, or validation studies in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence does not describe any peer review of the search strategy or the process/tool used (e.g., PRESS).

The manuscript does not report whether the search structure was or was not based on PICO, nor does it describe any alternative conceptual structure or explorations used to develop it in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Screening was performed independently by two systematic reviewers.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers (two) performing screening, but does not specify this number separately for different screening stages (e.g., title/abstract screening vs full-text review).

elements.quote: Screening was performed independently by two systematic reviewers.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that screening was performed independently, indicating independent reviewer work at the screening stage.

elements.quote: Any disagreements were resolved via consensus or a third reviewer.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process used to resolve screening disagreements (consensus or adjudication by a third reviewer).
No information is provided about processes to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators.

elements.quote: Non-­ English articles were translated using Google Translate and assessed by a systematic reviewer with good knowledge of the language.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the method used to translate non-English articles (Google Translate) and how translated items were assessed.

elements.quote: The data were managed using the review software Rayyan.
elements.reason: The authors report use of the Rayyan review software to manage screening data, indicating integration of an automation/review management tool into the selection process.
There is no information identifying externally derived classifiers by version or reference, nor reporting records removed pre-screening or their role.
No details are provided about internally derived classifiers, their use, training, or validation.
No description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules is provided.
No information on use of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection is reported.
No description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records (or how they were derived) is present in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Data extraction was performed by one systematic reviewer and checked by a second reviewer.
elements.reason: Explicitly states the number of reviewers involved in data extraction (one extractor, one checker).

elements.quote: Data extraction was performed by one systematic reviewer and checked by a second reviewer.
elements.reason: Indicates that two reviewers were involved and that one performed extraction while the other checked, implying multiple data collectors and their roles.

elements.quote: Disagreements were resolved through consensus.
elements.reason: Describes the process used to resolve disagreements between data collectors (consensus).
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes to obtain/confirm data from investigators in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Data extraction was performed using Microsoft Excel.
elements.reason: Although Excel is mentioned as the tool used for data extraction, there is no description of any automation tools (their use, training, or validation). Therefore the criterion about automation tools is not met.

elements.quote: Non-­ English articles were translated using Google Translate and assessed by a systematic reviewer with good knowledge of the language.
elements.reason: Describes the method used to translate non-English articles (Google Translate) and subsequent assessment by a reviewer with language knowledge.
No software for extracting data from figures is specified in the provided evidence.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies across reports are described in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Data extracted included study design, population characteristics, outcomes, prevalence, duration of symptoms and risk factors.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists outcomes broadly (eg, 'outcomes', 'prevalence', 'duration of symptoms', 'risk factors') but does not provide definitions for the specific outcome domains or define what each outcome domain encompasses.

elements.quote: Without a clear, internationally agreed case definition, we included studies that reported symptoms or outcomes assessed at 12 or more weeks post COVID-­ 19 onset.
elements.reason: The time frame for measurement of outcomes is explicitly specified (assessments at 12 or more weeks post onset).
No statement was found declaring whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (eg all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.
There is no description of a process used to select among multiple compatible results within outcome domains (eg rules for choosing measures or time points) when not all were sought.
No reporting of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance, nor rationales for any such changes, is present in the provided evidence.
No reporting of changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains, or rationales for changes, is present in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not identify which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions nor provide rationale for any prioritisation.

elements.quote: Data extracted included study design, population characteristics, outcomes, prevalence, duration of symptoms and risk factors.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists several variables that were extracted (study design, population characteristics, outcomes, prevalence, duration of symptoms, risk factors) but does not provide definitions for these variables or a comprehensive list of all other variables (e.g., funding sources, detailed participant or intervention characteristic definitions).
No text in the provided evidence describes assumptions made about missing or unclear study information (no explicit statement of assumptions or rules for handling missing/unclear data was found).

elements.quote: A data extraction template informed by a previous review 20 was reviewed, updated and piloted before being finalised.
elements.reason: The authors state they used a data extraction template informed by a previous review (cited as 20), indicating a cited tool/process was used to determine which data items to collect.

elements.quote: The included studies were assessed for risk of bias using the tool produced by Hoy et al 21 (online supplemental file 2). This assessment checklist is a validated tool for assessing risk of bias in prevalence studies.
elements.reason: An existing risk-of-bias tool (Hoy et al) is named and described as validated, but no version number or detailed citation/version information is provided.

elements.quote: The checklist has 10 domains for assessing risk of bias, used to calculate a cumulative overall risk of bias for the whole study.
elements.reason: The evidence states the tool has 10 domains, but the specific domains, components, or individual items are not listed or described in the provided text.

elements.quote: The checklist has 10 domains for assessing risk of bias, used to calculate a cumulative overall risk of bias for the whole study.
elements.reason: The text indicates an overall cumulative risk-of-bias judgement was calculated, but it does not report the explicit rules or criteria used to derive the overall judgement.
No description of any adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The included studies were assessed for risk of bias using the tool produced by Hoy et al 21 (online supplemental file 2). This assessment checklist is a validated tool for assessing risk of bias in prevalence studies.
elements.reason: A previously published tool (Hoy et al) was used; there is no indication that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created for this review.

The retrieved evidence does not report how many reviewers assessed risk of bias for included studies, whether they worked independently, or the procedures for resolving disagreements specific to risk-of-bias assessment.
There is no information in the provided evidence about processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.

elements.quote: The data were managed using the review software Rayyan. 19
elements.reason: No automation tools are described as being used for risk-of-bias assessment. The mention of Rayyan refers to screening management, not to automated risk-of-bias assessment, and no training/validation/use details for such tools are provided.

elements.quote: Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that symptom outcomes were presented as proportions with 95% CIs and describes the meta-analytic model used for pooling, specifying the effect measure (proportion) and its CI estimation method.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size (e.g., categorizations of small/medium/large effects) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the impact of high risk of bias studies and statistical methods, Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation using inverse variance meta-analysis, on the estimates.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes a specific transformation (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine) and inverse-variance meta-analysis as a sensitivity approach, which is a method to re-express/transform synthesized proportion results.

Although the authors justify the choice of meta-analytic model due to heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes, there is no explicit justification reported for the choice of the effect measure itself (that is, why proportions were chosen as the effect measure).

elements.quote: If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes. ... We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non-­ hospitalised or a mix of both populations if no subset data were available. Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state the rule used to decide which studies were synthesised quantitatively (meta-analysis performed when two or more studies reported a symptom) and describe grouping by setting and symptom clusters for synthesis; thus processes for deciding eligibility for each synthesis are described.

elements.quote: Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. 22 If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes. 23 24 Heterogeneity between estimates was assessed using the I 2 statistic. 25 Additional subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the modification of the following factors on proportion of symptoms: hospitalisation, settings, continents and follow-­ up timing. We also conducted meta-­ regression analysis on the percentage of females and intensive care unit (ICU) patients where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the impact of high risk of bias studies and statistical methods, Freeman-­ Tukey double arcsine transformation using inverse variance meta-­ analysis, on the estimates. Funnel plots were plotted using proportion of the symptom against the precision and sample sizes 22 where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom to explore risk of publication bias. All analysis and data presentation were performed using metaprop 26 and ggplot2 27 in R (V.4.0.5) via RStudio (V.1.3.1093). 28 The data are presented using a combination of infographics, prepared by a design company (Design Science 29 ) and scientific tables to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non-­ specialists.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes several data-preparation and analysis methods (estimation of proportions and 95% CIs using the exact method; random intercept logistic regression meta-analysis with Hartung–Knapp; I2 for heterogeneity; meta-regression; sensitivity analyses including Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation; software used). However, it does not explicitly describe all data-preparation steps such as handling of missing summary statistics or detailed data conversion procedures across studies, so the reporting is incomplete.

elements.quote: The data are presented using a combination of infographics, prepared by a design company (Design Science ) and scientific tables to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non- specialists.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that 'scientific tables' were used to present data, but does not describe the tabular structures themselves or the specific data fields/columns included in those tables. Therefore description is present but incomplete.

elements.quote: Funnel plots were plotted using proportion of the symptom against the precision and sample sizes where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom to explore risk of publication bias. All analysis and data presentation were performed using metaprop and ggplot2 in R (V.4.0.5) via RStudio (V.1.3.1093). The data are presented using a combination of infographics, prepared by a design company (Design Science ) and scientific tables to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non- specialists.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly describe graphical methods used: funnel plots (with axes specified), use of ggplot2 for plotting, and use of infographics for presentation, satisfying description of graphical methods.

elements.quote: We presented symptom proportions by different settings, as presented in the individual studies: hospitalised, non- hospitalised or a mix of both populations if no subset data were available. Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the basis for grouping studies/entries in presentations: by setting (hospitalised, non-hospitalised, mixed) and by symptom clusters (physiological groupings).

elements.quote: The data are presented using a combination of infographics, prepared by a design company (Design Science ) and scientific tables to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non- specialists.
elements.reason: The manuscript gives a rationale for using infographics (non-standard graphs) — to facilitate interpretation by different stakeholders, including non-specialists.

elements.quote: All analysis and data presentation were performed using metaprop 26 and ggplot2 27 in R (V.4.0.5) via RStudio (V.1.3.1093). 28
elements.reason: Software packages and version numbers (metaprop, ggplot2, R v4.0.5, RStudio v1.3.1093) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: The remaining studies include single symptoms or imaging and diagnostics and are presented narratively.
elements.reason: The authors state that studies not included in meta-analysis were presented narratively, which describes the alternative synthesis method, but no detailed justification is provided for why narrative synthesis was chosen beyond this statement.

elements.quote: If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes.
elements.reason: The meta-analysis model (random intercept logistic regression) and the rationale for its choice (heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification ... Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. ... Sensitivity analyses were conducted ... Freeman-­ Tukey double arcsine transformation using inverse variance meta-­ analysis, on the estimates.
elements.reason: The statistical methods are described: random intercept logistic regression with Hartung-Knapp modification, exact method for CIs, and sensitivity use of Freeman-Tukey transformation with inverse-variance meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity between estimates was assessed using the I 2 statistic.
elements.reason: The method used to identify/quantify statistical heterogeneity (I^2 statistic) is explicitly reported.

elements.quote: If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes.
elements.reason: Although a random-effects model is specified, no between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is named in the provided text.

elements.quote: a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification due to the heterogeneity and skewed sample sizes.
elements.reason: The use of the Hartung-Knapp modification (a method for calculating CIs for the summary effect) is reported.

elements.quote: Symptoms were broadly grouped into physiological clusters through discussion with clinicians. Proportion of symptoms and its 95% CIs were estimated using the exact method. ... Additional subgroup analysis was conducted ... We also conducted meta-­ regression analysis on the percentage of females and intensive care unit (ICU) patients where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the impact of high risk of bias studies and statistical methods ...
elements.reason: Other implementation details relevant to random-effects analyses are provided (symptom grouping, exact method for proportions, subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses).

elements.quote: If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed using a random intercept logistic regression model with Hartung-­ Knapp modification ...
elements.reason: No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed or described in the manuscript; methods reported are frequentist, so reporting Bayesian priors is not applicable.

elements.quote: We undertook individual descriptive analysis for each study. ... If there were two or more studies for each symptom, a meta-­ analysis was performed ...
elements.reason: There is no description of methods to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multivariate models, robust variance estimation).

elements.quote: The remaining studies include single symptoms or imaging and diagnostics and are presented narratively.
elements.reason: While the authors note some studies were presented narratively, they do not explicitly identify planned syntheses that were judged impossible/inappropriate nor provide explicit reasons beyond reporting format.

elements.quote: Additional subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the modification of the following factors on proportion of symptoms: hospitalisation, settings, continents and follow-­ up timing. We also conducted meta-­ regression analysis on the percentage of females and intensive care unit (ICU) patients where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom.
elements.reason: The methods used to explore heterogeneity are explicitly specified: subgroup analyses (with listed factors) and meta-regression (on % female and % ICU patients).

elements.quote: Additional subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the modification of the following factors on proportion of symptoms: hospitalisation, settings, continents and follow-­ up timing. We also conducted meta-­ regression analysis on the percentage of females and intensive care unit (ICU) patients where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom.
elements.reason: Factors and some factor levels are reported (e.g. hospitalisation status, settings, continents, follow-up timing; % females, % ICU patients). However, the expected direction of effect modification is not reported.

elements.quote: We also conducted meta-­ regression analysis on the percentage of females and intensive care unit (ICU) patients where there were more than 10 studies for the symptom.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates use of study-level variables in meta-regression (percentage of females, percentage ICU patients), but it does not state whether within-study contrasts were used or whether both approaches were applied.

elements.quote: Additional subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the modification of the following factors on proportion of symptoms: hospitalisation, settings, continents and follow-­ up timing. ... Heterogeneity between estimates was assessed using the I 2 statistic.
elements.reason: Subgroup analyses are reported and heterogeneity assessment (I2) is described, but specific methods for formally comparing subgroup effects (e.g. tests for interaction or comparison procedures) are not described.

elements.quote: We undertook individual descriptive analysis for each study. elements.quote: A deeper understanding of long COVID is currently prevented by the limitations of the published literature. The studies included in our review were highly heterogeneous due to differences in their study designs, settings, populations, follow-­ up time and symptom ascertainment methods. In addition, studies used inconsistent terminology describing symptoms and limited details and stratification on pre-­ existing comorbidities, the severity of COVID-­ 19 and treatment methods. This inconsistency and limited reporting partly explain the high degree of variability observed. The lack of case-control studies prevent a direct attribution of symptoms solely to COVID-­ 19; larger prospective studies with matched control groups are needed. ... The majority of long COVID cohorts were conducted in Western Europe on patients recently discharged from hospital. There is a paucity of evidence on the long-­ term effects of COVID-­ 19 in low-­ to-­ middle income countries and in people who were not hospitalised. Similarly, there were no studies identified focusing on children, despite evidence showing that children and young people are also affected by long COVID. 74 Additionally, no study stratified by ethnicity, an important risk factor for the acute phase.
